# polkadot_erasure_coding - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-erasure-coding/^26.0.0/

## Expand description

As part of Polkadot’s availability system, certain pieces of data for each block are required to be kept available.

The way we accomplish this is by erasure coding the data into n pieces and constructing a merkle root of the data.

Each of n validators stores their piece of data. We assume `n = 3f + k`, `0 < k ≤ 3`.
f is the maximum number of faulty validators in the system.
The data is coded so any f+1 chunks can be used to reconstruct the full data.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Branches](https://docs.rs/struct.Branches.html)
- An iterator that yields merkle branches and chunk data for all chunks to be sent to other validators.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Errors in erasure coding.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [branch_](https://docs.rs/fn.branch_hash.html)- hash
- Verify a merkle branch, yielding the chunk hash meant to be present at that index.
- [branches](https://docs.rs/fn.branches.html)
- Construct a trie from chunks of an erasure-coded value. This returns the root hash and an iterator of merkle proofs, one for each validator.
- [obtain_](https://docs.rs/fn.obtain_chunks.html)- chunks
- Obtain erasure-coded chunks, one for each validator.
- [obtain_](https://docs.rs/fn.obtain_chunks_v1.html)- chunks_ - v1
- Obtain erasure-coded chunks for v1 `AvailableData`, one for each validator.
- [reconstruct](https://docs.rs/fn.reconstruct.html)
- Reconstruct decodable data from a set of chunks.
- [reconstruct_](https://docs.rs/fn.reconstruct_from_systematic.html)- from_ - systematic
- Reconstruct the available data from the set of systematic chunks.
- [reconstruct_](https://docs.rs/fn.reconstruct_from_systematic_v1.html)- from_ - systematic_ - v1
- Reconstruct the v1 available data from the set of systematic chunks.
- [reconstruct_](https://docs.rs/fn.reconstruct_v1.html)- v1
- Reconstruct the v1 available data from a set of chunks.
- [recovery_](https://docs.rs/fn.recovery_threshold.html)- threshold
- Obtain a threshold of chunks that should be enough to recover the data.
- [systematic_](https://docs.rs/fn.systematic_recovery_threshold.html)- recovery_ - threshold
- Obtain the threshold of systematic chunks that should be enough to recover the data.

# polkadot_node_primitives - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-primitives/^26.0.0/

## Expand description

Primitive types used on the node-side.

Unlike the `polkadot-primitives` crate, these primitives are only used on the node-side,
not shared between the node and the runtime. This crate builds on top of the primitives defined
there.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DISPUTE_](https://docs.rs/constant.DISPUTE_CANDIDATE_LIFETIME_AFTER_FINALIZATION.html)- CANDIDATE_ - LIFETIME_ - AFTER_ - FINALIZATION
- How many blocks after finalization an information about backed/included candidate should be pre-loaded (when scraping onchain votes) and kept locally (when pruning).
- [DISPUTE_](https://docs.rs/constant.DISPUTE_WINDOW.html)- WINDOW
- It would be nice to draw this from the chain state, but we have no tools for it right now. On Polkadot this is 1 day, and on Kusama it’s 6 hours.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_FINALITY_LAG.html)- FINALITY_ - LAG
- Linked to `MAX_FINALITY_LAG`in relay chain selection,`MAX_HEADS_LOOK_BACK`in`approval-voting`and`MAX_BATCH_SCRAPE_ANCESTORS`in`dispute-coordinator`
- [NODE_](https://docs.rs/constant.NODE_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- The current node version, which takes the basic SemVer form `<major>.<minor>.<patch>`. In general, minor should be bumped on every release while major or patch releases are relatively rare.
- [POV_](https://docs.rs/constant.POV_BOMB_LIMIT.html)- BOMB_ - LIMIT
- The bomb limit for decompressing PoV blobs.
- [VALIDATION_](https://docs.rs/constant.VALIDATION_CODE_BOMB_LIMIT.html)- CODE_ - BOMB_ - LIMIT - Deprecated
- The bomb limit for decompressing code blobs.

# polkadot_node_subsystem_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-types/^32.0.0/

## Expand description

Subsystem trait definitions and message types.

Node-side logic for Polkadot is mostly comprised of Subsystems, which are discrete components that communicate via message-passing. They are coordinated by an overseer, provided by a separate crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Activated](https://docs.rs/struct.ActivatedLeaf.html)- Leaf
- Activated leaf.
- [Active](https://docs.rs/struct.ActiveLeavesUpdate.html)- Leaves - Update
- Changes in the set of active leaves: the parachain heads which we care to work on.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultSubsystemClient.html)- Subsystem - Client
- Default implementation of `RuntimeApiSubsystemClient`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Overseer](https://docs.rs/enum.OverseerSignal.html)- Signal
- Signals sent by an overseer to a subsystem.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chain](https://docs.rs/trait.ChainApiBackend.html)- ApiBackend
- Offers header utilities.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/trait.RuntimeApiSubsystemClient.html)- ApiSubsystem - Client
- Exposes all runtime calls that are used by the runtime API subsystem.

- Block type.

- The block number type used by Polkadot. 32-bits will allow for 136 years of blocks assuming 1 block per second.

# polkadot_overseer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-overseer/^32.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overseer)Overseer

`overseer` implements the Overseer architecture described in the
[implementers’ guide](https://paritytech.github.io/polkadot-sdk/book/node/overseer.html).
For the motivations behind implementing the overseer itself you should
check out that guide, documentation in this crate will be mostly discussing
technical stuff.

An `Overseer` is something that allows spawning/stopping and overseeing
asynchronous tasks as well as establishing a well-defined and easy to use
protocol that the tasks can use to communicate with each other. It is desired
that this protocol is the only way tasks communicate with each other, however
at this moment there are no foolproof guards against other ways of communication.

The `Overseer` is instantiated with a pre-defined set of `Subsystems` that
share the same behavior from `Overseer`’s point of view.

```
                             +-----------------------------+
                             |         Overseer            |
                             +-----------------------------+
            ................|  Overseer "holds" these and uses |..............
            .                  them to (re)start things                      .
            .                                                                .
            .  +-------------------+                +---------------------+  .
            .  |   Subsystem1      |                |   Subsystem2        |  .
            .  +-------------------+                +---------------------+  .
            .           |                                       |            .
            ..................................................................
                        |                                       |
                      start()                                 start()
                        V                                       V
            ..................| Overseer "runs" these |.......................
            .  +--------------------+               +---------------------+  .
            .  | SubsystemInstance1 |               | SubsystemInstance2  |  .
            .  +--------------------+               +---------------------+  .
            ..................................................................
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use self::metrics::`- [Metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/struct.Metrics.html)as OverseerMetrics;
- `pub use self::dummy::`- [DummySubsystem](https://docs.rs/dummy/struct.DummySubsystem.html);
- `pub use polkadot_node_metrics::metrics::`- [prometheus](https://docs.rs/metrics/metrics/prometheus/index.html);
- `pub use`- [orchestra](https://docs.rs/orchestra/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/orchestra/index.html)as gen;

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Blake](https://docs.rs/struct.BlakeTwo256.html)- Two256
- Blake2-256 Hash implementation.
- [Candidate](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateHash.html)- Hash
- Unit type wrapper around `Hash`
- [Head](https://docs.rs/struct.HeadData.html)- Data
- Parachain head data included in the chain.
- [Hrmp](https://docs.rs/struct.HrmpChannelId.html)- Channel - Id
- A type that uniquely identifies an HRMP channel. An HRMP channel is established between two
paras. In text, we use the notation `(A, B)`to specify a channel between A and B. The channels are unidirectional, meaning that`(A, B)`and`(B, A)`refer to different channels. The convention is that we use the first item tuple for the sender and the second for the recipient. Only one channel is allowed between two participants in one direction, i.e. there cannot be 2 different channels identified by`(A, B)`. A channel with the same para id in sender and recipient is invalid. That is, however, not enforced.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- Unique identifier of a parachain.
- [Inbound](https://docs.rs/struct.InboundDownwardMessage.html)- Downward - Message
- A wrapped version of `DownwardMessage`. The difference is that it has attached the block number when the message was sent.
- [Inbound](https://docs.rs/struct.InboundHrmpMessage.html)- Hrmp - Message
- An HRMP message seen from the perspective of a recipient.
- [Outbound](https://docs.rs/struct.OutboundHrmpMessage.html)- Hrmp - Message
- An HRMP message seen from the perspective of a sender.
- [Slot](https://docs.rs/struct.Slot.html)
- Unit type wrapper that represents a slot.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationCode.html)- Code
- Parachain validation code.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationCodeHash.html)- Code - Hash
- Unit type wrapper around `Hash`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountId.html)- Id
- Alias to the opaque account ID type for this chain, actually a `AccountId32`. This is always 32 bytes.
- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountIndex.html)- Index
- The type for looking up accounts. We don’t expect more than 4 billion of them.
- [Account](https://docs.rs/type.AccountPublic.html)- Public
- Alias to the public key used for this chain, actually a `MultiSigner`. Like the signature, this also isn’t a fixed size when encoded, as different cryptos have different size public keys.
- [Authority](https://docs.rs/type.AuthorityDiscoveryId.html)- Discovery - Id
- An authority discovery authority identifier.
- [Balance](https://docs.rs/type.Balance.html)
- The balance of an account.
128-bits (or 38 significant decimal figures) will allow for 10 m currency (`10^7`) at a resolution to all for one second’s worth of an annualised 50% reward be paid to a unit holder (`10^11`unit denomination), or`10^18`total atomic units, to grow at 50%/year for 51 years (`10^9`multiplier) for an eventual total of`10^27`units (27 significant decimal figures). We round denomination to`10^12`(12 SDF), and leave the other redundancy at the upper end so that 32 bits may be multiplied with a balance in 128 bits without worrying about overflow.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/type.Block.html)
- Block type.
- [BlockId](https://docs.rs/type.BlockId.html)
- Block ID.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/type.BlockNumber.html)- Number
- The block number type used by Polkadot. 32-bits will allow for 136 years of blocks assuming 1 block per second.
- [Downward](https://docs.rs/type.DownwardMessage.html)- Message
- A message sent from the relay-chain down to a parachain.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/type.Hash.html)
- A hash of some data used by the relay chain.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/type.Header.html)
- Header type.
- [Horizontal](https://docs.rs/type.HorizontalMessages.html)- Messages
- [Moment](https://docs.rs/type.Moment.html)
- An instant or duration in time.
- [Nonce](https://docs.rs/type.Nonce.html)
- Index of a transaction in the relay chain. 32-bit should be plenty.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/type.SessionIndex.html)- Index
- Simple index type with which we can count sessions.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/type.Signature.html)
- Alias to type for a signature for a transaction on the relay chain. This allows one of several kinds of underlying crypto to be used, so isn’t a fixed size when encoded.
- [Upward](https://docs.rs/type.UpwardMessage.html)- Message
- A message from a parachain to its Relay Chain.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

- [distributions](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Error type of random number generators

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait used to indicate that an `RngCore``BlockRngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- An automatically-implemented extension trait on `RngCore`
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- The core of a random number generator.
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `std`and- `std_rng`
- Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)- rng - `std`and- `std_rng`
- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# schnellru - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/schnellru/^0.2.3/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#a-fast-and-flexible-lru-map)A fast and flexible LRU map

This repository contains a fast and flexible LRU map.

- Blazingly fast. Up to twice as fast as the `lru`
- Can be also used as an ordered map, with roughly the same performance as `indexmap``indexmap`only supports O(n) non-perturbing removals).
- Customizable. Out-of-box can be limited by length or by memory usage, but supports custom limiters which can be made to limit the map by whatever you want.
- Tested, miri-clean, clippy-clean and fuzzed.
- Supports `no_std`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use schnellru::{LruMap, ByLength};
let mut map = LruMap::new(ByLength::new(3));
// Insert three elements.
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
map.insert(3, "three");
assert_eq!(map.len(), 3);
// They're ordered according to which one was inserted last.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&2, &"two"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
// Access the least recently inserted one.
assert_eq!(*map.get(&1).unwrap(), "one");
// Now the order's changed.
// The element we've accessed was moved to the front.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&2, &"two"));
// Insert a fourth element.
// This will automatically pop the least recently accessed one.
map.insert(4, "four");
// Still the same number of elements.
assert_eq!(map.len(), 3);
// And this is the one which was removed.
assert!(map.peek(&2).is_none());
// And here's the new order.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&4, &"four"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ByLength](https://docs.rs/struct.ByLength.html)
- A limiter for a map which is limited by the number of elements.
- [ByMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.ByMemoryUsage.html)- Usage
- A limiter for a map which is limited by memory usage.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHasher.html)- Hasher
- The default hasher used by the LRU map.
- [Drain](https://docs.rs/struct.Drain.html)
- A drain iterator for the LRU map.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator for the LRU map.
- [IterMut](https://docs.rs/struct.IterMut.html)
- An mutable iterator for the LRU map, values are mutable.
- [LruMap](https://docs.rs/struct.LruMap.html)
- An LRU hash map.
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomState.html)- State
- The default hash builder used by the LRU map.
- [Unlimited](https://docs.rs/struct.Unlimited.html)
- A limiter for a map which can hold an unlimited number of elements.
- [Unlimited](https://docs.rs/struct.UnlimitedCompact.html)- Compact
- A limiter for a map which can hold an unlimited** number of elements.

- [Limiter](https://docs.rs/trait.Limiter.html)
- A trait used to customize the behavior and the limits of the LRU map.

# sp_application_crypto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-application-crypto/^48.0.0/

## Expand description

Traits and macros for constructing application specific strongly typed crypto wrappers.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ecdsa](https://docs.rs/ecdsa/index.html)
- Ecdsa crypto types.
- [ed25519](https://docs.rs/ed25519/index.html)
- Ed25519 crypto types.
- [key_](https://docs.rs/key_types/index.html)- types
- Known key types; this also functions as a global registry of key types for projects wishing to avoid collisions with each other.
- [sr25519](https://docs.rs/sr25519/index.html)
- Sr25519 crypto types.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [app_](https://docs.rs/macro.app_crypto.html)- crypto
- Declares `Public`,`Pair`,`Signature`and`ProofOfPossession`types which are functionally equivalent to the corresponding types defined by`$module`but are new application-specific types whose identifier is`$key_type`.
- [app_](https://docs.rs/macro.app_crypto_pair_common.html)- crypto_ - pair_ - common
- Declares `Pair`type which is functionally equivalent to`$pair`, but is new application-specific type whose identifier is`$key_type`. It is a common part shared between full_crypto and non full_crypto environments.
- [with_](https://docs.rs/macro.with_pair.html)- pair
- Generate the given code if the pair type is available.
- [wrap](https://docs.rs/macro.wrap.html)
- Implement bidirectional `From`and on-way`AsRef`/`AsMut`for two types,`$inner`and`$outer`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/struct.CryptoTypeId.html)- Type - Id
- An identifier for a specific cryptographic algorithm used by a key pair
- [KeyType](https://docs.rs/struct.KeyTypeId.html)- Id
- An identifier for a type of cryptographic key.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Derive](https://docs.rs/enum.DeriveJunction.html)- Junction
- A since derivation junction description. It is the single parameter used when creating
a new secret key from an existing secret key and, in the case of `SoftRaw`and`SoftIndex`a new public key from an existing public key.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AppCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.AppCrypto.html)
- Application-specific cryptographic object.
- [AppPair](https://docs.rs/trait.AppPair.html)
- Application-specific key pair.
- [AppPublic](https://docs.rs/trait.AppPublic.html)
- Application-specific public key.
- [AppSignature](https://docs.rs/trait.AppSignature.html)
- Application-specific signature and Proof Of Possession
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/trait.BoundToRuntimeAppPublic.html)- ToRuntime - AppPublic
- Something that is bound to a fixed `RuntimeAppPublic`
- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/trait.MaybeHash.html)- Hash
- Type which implements Hash in std, not when no-std (std variant).
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/trait.RuntimeAppPublic.html)- AppPublic
- Runtime interface for an application’s public key.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/trait.RuntimePublic.html)- Public
- Runtime interface for a public key.
- [Ss58](https://docs.rs/trait.Ss58Codec.html)- Codec
- Key that can be encoded to/from SS58.

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^1.0.64/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`by hand, and switching from handwritten impls to thiserror or vice versa is not a breaking change.
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display`impl is generated for your error if you provide`#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {})", i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From`impl is generated for each variant that contains a`#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()`method is implemented to return whichever field has a`#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()`method is implemented to provide whichever field has a type named`Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace`. Using`Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()`method is forwarded to the source’s`provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and Display methods straight through to an underlying error without adding an additional message. This would be appropriate for enums that need an “anything else” variant.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

---

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3.8.1/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/target-redirect/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/

## Expand description

Utility module for subsystems

Many subsystems have common interests such as canceling a bunch of spawned jobs, or determining what their validator ID is. These common interests are factored into this module.

This crate also reexports Prometheus metric types which are expected to be implemented by subsystems.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [availability_](https://docs.rs/availability_chunks/index.html)- chunks
- Helpers for the validator->chunk index mapping.
- [backing_](https://docs.rs/backing_implicit_view/index.html)- implicit_ - view
- A utility for managing the implicit view of the relay-chain derived from active leaves and the minimum allowed relay-parents that parachain candidates can have and be backed in those leaves’ children.
- [database](https://docs.rs/database/index.html)
- Database trait for subsystem. Database trait for polkadot db.
- [inclusion_](https://docs.rs/inclusion_emulator/index.html)- emulator
- An emulator for node-side code to predict the results of on-chain parachain inclusion and predict future constraints.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- This module reexports Prometheus types and defines the `Metrics`
- [nesting_](https://docs.rs/nesting_sender/index.html)- sender
- Nested message sending
- [reexports](https://docs.rs/reexports/index.html)
- These reexports are required so that external crates can use the `delegated_subsystem`macro properly.
- [reputation](https://docs.rs/reputation/index.html)
- A utility abstraction to collect and send reputation changes.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_relay_parent_session.html)- relay_ - parent_ - session
- Check whether a relay parent is valid in a given session.
- [choose_](https://docs.rs/fn.choose_random_subset.html)- random_ - subset
- Choose a random subset of `min`elements. But always include`is_priority`elements.
- [choose_](https://docs.rs/fn.choose_random_subset_with_rng.html)- random_ - subset_ - with_ - rng
- Choose a random subset of `min`elements using a specific Random Generator`Rng`But always include`is_priority`elements.
- [determine_](https://docs.rs/fn.determine_new_blocks.html)- new_ - blocks
- Given a new chain-head hash, this determines the hashes of all new blocks we should track metadata for, given this head.
- [executor_](https://docs.rs/fn.executor_params_at_relay_parent.html)- params_ - at_ - relay_ - parent
- Requests executor parameters from the runtime effective at given relay-parent. First obtains
session index at the relay-parent, relying on the fact that it should be cached by the runtime
API caching layer even if the block itself has already been pruned. Then requests executor
parameters by session index.
Returns an error if failed to communicate to the runtime, or the parameters are not in the
storage, which should never happen.
Returns default execution parameters if the runtime doesn’t yet support `SessionExecutorParams`API call. Otherwise, returns execution parameters returned by the runtime.
- [fetch_](https://docs.rs/fn.fetch_relay_parent_info.html)- relay_ - parent_ - info
- Fetch relay parent info for a block, including the block being queried at.
- [find_](https://docs.rs/fn.find_validator_group.html)- validator_ - group
- Find the validator group the given validator index belongs to.
- [gen_](https://docs.rs/fn.gen_ratio.html)- ratio
- Returns a `bool`with a probability of`a / b`of being true.
- [gen_](https://docs.rs/fn.gen_ratio_rng.html)- ratio_ - rng
- Returns a `bool`with a probability of`a / b`of being true.
- [has_](https://docs.rs/fn.has_required_runtime.html)- required_ - runtime
- Verifies if `ParachainHost`runtime api is at least at version`required_runtime_version`. This method is used to determine if a given runtime call is supported by the runtime.
- [request_](https://docs.rs/fn.request_approval_voting_params.html)- approval_ - voting_ - params
- Request `ApprovalVotingParams`from the runtime

# polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/index.html

## Expand description

Utility module for subsystems

Many subsystems have common interests such as canceling a bunch of spawned jobs, or determining what their validator ID is. These common interests are factored into this module.

This crate also reexports Prometheus metric types which are expected to be implemented by subsystems.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [availability_](https://docs.rs/availability_chunks/index.html)- chunks
- Helpers for the validator->chunk index mapping.
- [backing_](https://docs.rs/backing_implicit_view/index.html)- implicit_ - view
- A utility for managing the implicit view of the relay-chain derived from active leaves and the minimum allowed relay-parents that parachain candidates can have and be backed in those leaves’ children.
- [database](https://docs.rs/database/index.html)
- Database trait for subsystem. Database trait for polkadot db.
- [inclusion_](https://docs.rs/inclusion_emulator/index.html)- emulator
- An emulator for node-side code to predict the results of on-chain parachain inclusion and predict future constraints.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- This module reexports Prometheus types and defines the `Metrics`
- [nesting_](https://docs.rs/nesting_sender/index.html)- sender
- Nested message sending
- [reexports](https://docs.rs/reexports/index.html)
- These reexports are required so that external crates can use the `delegated_subsystem`macro properly.
- [reputation](https://docs.rs/reputation/index.html)
- A utility abstraction to collect and send reputation changes.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Convenient and efficient runtime info access. Convenient interface to runtime information.
- [vstaging](https://docs.rs/vstaging/index.html)
- Helpers for working with unreleased runtime calls Contains helpers for staging runtime calls.

[152](#152)impl TryFrom<crate::runtime::Error> for Error {
[153](#153)	type Error = ();
[154](#154)
[155](#155)	fn try_from(e: crate::runtime::Error) -> Result<Self, ()> {
[156](#156)		use crate::runtime::Error;
[157](#157)
[158](#158)		match e {
[159](#159)			Error::RuntimeRequestCanceled(e) => Ok(Self::Oneshot(e)),
[160](#160)			Error::RuntimeRequest(e) => Ok(Self::RuntimeApi(e)),
[161](#161)			Error::NoSuchSession(_) => Err(()),
[162](#162)		}
[163](#163)	}

[560](#560)pub fn choose_random_subset_with_rng<T, F: FnMut(&T) -> bool, R: rand::Rng>(
[563](#563)	is_priority: F,
[564](#564)	v: &mut Vec<T>,

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/0.9.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/index.html

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distr](https://docs.rs/distr/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `RngCore`
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Types which may be filled with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- User-level interface for RNGs
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)
- Implementation-level interface for RNGs
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRngCore`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRngCore.html)- Core
- A potentially fallible variant of `RngCore`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill](https://docs.rs/fn.fill.html)- `thread_rng`
- Fill any type implementing `Fill`
- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value using the thread-local random number generator.

# polkadot_node_subsystem_util::nesting_sender - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/nesting_sender/index.html

## Expand description

Nested message sending

Useful for having mostly synchronous code, with submodules spawning short lived asynchronous tasks, sending messages back.

[§](https://docs.rs#background)Background

Writing concurrent and even multithreaded by default is inconvenient and slow: No references hence lots of needless cloning and data duplication, locks, mutexes, … We should reach for concurrency and parallelism when there is an actual need, not just because we can and it is reasonably safe in Rust.

I very much agree with many points in this blog post for example:

Another very good post by Pierre (Tomaka):

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

This module helps with this in part. It does not break the multithreaded by default approach,
but it breaks the `spawn everything` approach. So once you `spawn` you will still be
multithreaded by default, despite that for most tasks we spawn (which just wait for network or
some message to arrive), that is very much pointless and needless overhead. You will just spawn
less in the first place.

By default your code is single threaded, except when actually needed: - need to wait for long running synchronous IO (a threaded runtime is actually useful here) - need to wait for some async event (message to arrive) - need to do some hefty CPU bound processing (a thread is required here as well)

and it is not acceptable to block the main task for waiting for the result, because we actually really have other things to do or at least need to stay responsive just in case.

With the types and traits in this module you can achieve exactly that: You write modules which
just execute logic and can call into the functions of other modules - yes we are calling normal
functions. For the case a module you are calling into requires an occasional background task,
you provide it with a `NestingSender<M, ChildModuleMessage>` that it can pass to any spawned
tasks.

This way you don’t have to spawn a task for each module just for it to be able to handle asynchronous events. The module relies on the using/enclosing code/module to forward it any asynchronous messages in a structured way.

What makes this architecture nice is the separation of concerns - at the top you only have to provide a sender and dispatch received messages to the root module - it is completely irrelevant how complex that module is, it might consist of child modules also having the need to spawn and receive messages, which in turn do the same, still the root logic stays unchanged. Everything is isolated to the level where it belongs, while we still keep a single task scope in all non blocking/not CPU intensive parts, which allows us to share data via references for example.

Because the wrapping is optional and transparent to the lower modules, each module can also be used at the top directly without any wrapping, e.g. for standalone use or for testing purposes.

Checkout the documentation of [ NestingSender](https://docs.rs/struct.NestingSender.html) below for a basic
usage example. For a real world usage I would like to point you to the dispute-distribution
subsystem which makes use of this architecture.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Nothing is ever for free of course: Each level adds an indirect function call to message
sending. which should be cheap enough for most applications, but something to keep in mind. In
particular we avoided the use of of async traits, which would have required memory allocations
on each send. Also cloning of [ NestingSender](https://docs.rs/struct.NestingSender.html) is more
expensive than cloning a plain mpsc::Sender, the overhead should be negligible though.

Further limitations: Because everything is routed to the same channel, it is not possible with this approach to put back pressure on only a single source (as all are the same). If a module has a task that requires this, it indeed has to spawn a long running task which can do the back-pressure on that message source or we make it its own subsystem. This is just one of the situations that justifies the complexity of asynchrony.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Nesting](https://docs.rs/struct.NestingSender.html)- Sender
- A message sender that supports sending nested messages.

---

# Validator in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/struct.Validator.html

`pub struct Validator { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Local validator information

It can be created if the local node is a validator in the context of a particular relay chain block.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/lib.rs.html#609-629)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/lib.rs.html#609-629)

Get a struct representing this node’s validator if this node is in fact a validator in the context of the given block.

# CheckRelayParentSessionResult in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/enum.CheckRelayParentSessionResult.html

```
pub enum CheckRelayParentSessionResult {
    Valid,
    NotFound,
    NotSupported,
    RuntimeError(
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
}## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Valid)

### Valid

The relay parent is valid in the given session.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NotFound)

### NotFound

The relay parent was not found in the given session (or session mismatch in the self-query case).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NotSupported)

### NotSupported

The `ancestor_relay_parent_info` runtime API is not supported. Safe to
skip on old runtimes where cross-session relay parents don’t exist.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RuntimeError)

### RuntimeError([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

A runtime API or communication error occurred.

# check_relay_parent_session in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/fn.check_relay_parent_session.html

```
pub async fn check_relay_parent_session(
    sender: &mut impl
```
[SubsystemSender](https://docs.rs/orchestra/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/orchestra/trait.SubsystemSender.html)<[RuntimeApiMessage](https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-types/32.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_node_subsystem_types/messages/enum.RuntimeApiMessage.html)>,
    query_at: [Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
    session_index: [SessionIndex](https://docs.rs/sp-staking/45.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_staking/type.SessionIndex.html),
    relay_parent: [Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
) -> [CheckRelayParentSessionResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckRelayParentSessionResult.html)## Expand description

Check whether a relay parent is valid in a given session.

Works for all blocks within the `max_relay_parent_session_age` window,
including the block being queried at (the “self” case where
`query_at == relay_parent`). The `ancestor_relay_parent_info` runtime API
only works for ancestors (a block is not in its own `AllowedRelayParents`).
This utility handles the self case by verifying the session directly via
`session_index_for_child`.

---

}## Expand description

Utility errors

    Infallible([Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html)),
    Context([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    SubsystemStalled(&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)),
    FromOrigin {
        origin: &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
        source: [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html)>,
    },
}## Expand description

An error type that describes faults that may happen

These are:

- Channels being closed
- Subsystems dying when they are not expected to
- Subsystems not dying when they are told to die
- etc.

# determine_new_blocks in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/fn.determine_new_blocks.html

```
pub async fn determine_new_blocks<E, Sender>(
    sender:
```
[&mut Sender](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    is_known: impl [Fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.Fn.html)(&[Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), E>,
    head: [Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
    header: &[Header](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Header.html),
    lower_bound_number: [BlockNumber](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.BlockNumber.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<([Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html), [Header](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Header.html))>, E>## Expand description

Given a new chain-head hash, this determines the hashes of all new blocks we should track metadata for, given this head.

This is guaranteed to be a subset of the (inclusive) ancestry of `head` determined as all
blocks above the lower bound or above the highest known block, whichever is higher.
This is formatted in descending order by block height.

An implication of this is that if `head` itself is known or not above the lower bound,
then the returned list will be empty.

This may be somewhat expensive when first recovering from major sync.

---

# executor_params_at_relay_parent in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/fn.executor_params_at_relay_parent.html

```
pub async fn executor_params_at_relay_parent(
    relay_parent:
```
[Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
    sender: &mut impl [SubsystemSender](https://docs.rs/orchestra/0.4.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/orchestra/trait.SubsystemSender.html)<[RuntimeApiMessage](https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-types/32.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_node_subsystem_types/messages/enum.RuntimeApiMessage.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[ExecutorParams](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/v9/executor_params/struct.ExecutorParams.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)>## Expand description

Requests executor parameters from the runtime effective at given relay-parent. First obtains
session index at the relay-parent, relying on the fact that it should be cached by the runtime
API caching layer even if the block itself has already been pruned. Then requests executor
parameters by session index.
Returns an error if failed to communicate to the runtime, or the parameters are not in the
storage, which should never happen.
Returns default execution parameters if the runtime doesn’t yet support `SessionExecutorParams`
API call.
Otherwise, returns execution parameters returned by the runtime.

---

# fetch_relay_parent_info in polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/fn.fetch_relay_parent_info.html

```
pub async fn fetch_relay_parent_info<Sender>(
    sender:
```
[&mut Sender](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    query_at: [Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
    session_index: [SessionIndex](https://docs.rs/sp-staking/45.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_staking/type.SessionIndex.html),
    relay_parent: [Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[RelayParentInfo](https://docs.rs/polkadot-primitives/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_primitives/vstaging/struct.RelayParentInfo.html)<[Hash](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.Hash.html), [BlockNumber](https://docs.rs/polkadot-core-primitives/24.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/polkadot_core_primitives/type.BlockNumber.html)>>, [Error](https://docs.rs/runtime/enum.Error.html)>## Expand description

Fetch relay parent info for a block, including the block being queried at.

Works for all blocks within the `max_relay_parent_session_age` window,
including the self-query case (`query_at == relay_parent`). For ancestors,
uses the `ancestor_relay_parent_info` runtime API. For self, constructs the
answer from the block header and session check.

Requires both `RuntimeApiMessage` and `ChainApiMessage` senders.

---

@ac_behavior id=AC.SHELL.BODY.1 surface=AC.SHELL.CONFIGURE.1 manual=4
Phase 4 — diversion-backed section ordering for correct AC_REQUIRE semantics. configure_template  Oracle template loader for configure script generation. diagnostics Diagnostics system matching Autoconf warning/error taxonomy. diversion Diversion Manager for M4 expansion output ordering. fortran Fortran language support for Autoconf. frozen GNU M4 frozen file format support — NC.PERM.5 resolution. i18n Internationalization (i18n) — 24 languages, matching GNU Autoconf parity.
Court: CROSS.032 — i18n / localization (15+ languages) input_validate  Input validation and security sandbox — NC.PERM.2 resolution. languages Language support modules for Autoconf. m4_engine  M4 macro expansion engine for Autoconf — wraps m4-rs-core. m4sh m4sh: Shell-generation macro library for Autoconf. m4sh_init  M4sh initialization – shell portability preamble. m4sugar m4sugar: Convenience macro library for Autoconf M4 programming. profile Oracle profile management for autoconf-rs-core. shell_gen  Shell script generator for Autoconf. signal Signal handling for autoconf-rs — CROSS.040 resolution. site_file  Site file handling for config.site / site-lisp (stub). template Template substitution for AC_SUBST, AC_CONFIG_FILES (stub). trace Autoconf Trace Event System trace_cache  TraceLog event caching for autom4te/autoheader — panel mandate. libtool_script  A minimal but functional `libtool` wrapper script (autoconf-rs native, GNU-free). Emitted by
configure when the project uses LT_INIT/AC_PROG_LIBTOOL. Handles the common automake toolchain:
–mode=compile CC … -c src -o obj.lo   -> .libs/obj.o (PIC) + obj.o + obj.lo descriptor
–mode=link    CC … -o lib.la objs     -> .libs/lib.a (static) + .libs/lib.so (shared) + lib.la
–mode=link    CC … -o prog objs *.la  -> resolves .lo/.la and links the program
–mode=install / –mode=clean            -> best-effort copy / rm macro_overrides  m4 macro definitions injected AFTER aclocal.m4 (so they override the project’s third-party
definitions) and BEFORE configure.ac. autoconf-rs cannot yet correctly expand some standard
third-party macros (notably pkg.m4’s PKG_CHECK_MODULES, whose internals leak
`pkg_default`/`glib_minimum` -> shell syntax errors). We replace them with clean, self-contained
shell that does the real work: run pkg-config at configure time, set PFX_CFLAGS/PFX_LIBS, and
record `@PFX_CFLAGS@`/`@PFX_LIBS@` substitutions into conf_subst.sed (consumed when config files
are created, mirroring confdefs.h -> config.h).

---

# autoconf_rs_cli - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/autoconf-rs-cli/0.1.53/target-redirect/autoconf_rs_cli/

## Expand description

autoconf-rs-cli shared library.

Provides the CLI argument parsing harness used by all 8 Autoconf binaries. Each binary is a thin wrapper that delegates to autoconf-rs-core.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Common](https://docs.rs/struct.CommonOpts.html)- Opts
- Common CLI options shared across Autoconf tools.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_input.html)- input
- Read a file into a String, or return stdin contents if path is “-”.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_stdin.html)- stdin
- Read all of stdin into a String.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [CliResult](https://docs.rs/type.CliResult.html)
- Common result type for CLI operations.

---
